week02-3-prototyping.alt: A desk covered in felt pens, pom-poms, modelling clay and a sheet of sketched game ideas.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: A prototype is made of whatever is on the table. Nothing here takes more than a minute to change.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: Coloured buttons and foam triangles placed on a grid drawn in pencil on a sheet of paper.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: A grid, some buttons, a legend down the side: enough to play a turn and find out whether the rule works.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: A hand laying out coloured matchsticks above a flower of buttons on white paper.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: Start with the action the player repeats: lay it out, do it by hand, see whether it is worth doing twice.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: A circular maze drawn on blue card, scattered with googly eyes, counters and a torn paper square labelled MAP.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: Foundation: a space, the pieces that move in it, and one resource worth crossing it for.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: Yellow and orange paper tiles and green triangles arranged as platforms between two red rails on black card.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: Structure: the rails and platforms first. Weapons, vehicles and scoring are features, and each one brings ten more rules.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: Pipe cleaners and foam shapes laid on black card as a branching path between a start token and a goal disc.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: Formal details: add one rule, play it, keep it only if the game cannot work without it.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: Folded red paper strips over black card forming a side-on platform level, with a pipe-cleaner creature and hand-drawn pickup tokens.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: Refinement: the pickups and the enemy come last, one at a time, each tested and written up.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: Torn paper mountains standing up from a grey card base, with counters marking positions in the valley between them.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: Paper answers the design questions. How the terrain reads, and how it feels to move through, is a question for the digital build.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: Two sheets of marker sketches: labelled ability icons above, and three hand-drawn monster designs below.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: An aesthetic prototype: icons and characters drawn in minutes, to settle what the game looks like before anything is modelled.

week02-3-prototyping.alt: A modelling-clay character with a pipe-cleaner weapon, standing on blue card labelled Main Character.
week02-3-prototyping.caption: Build the toy first. If the character is not fun to pick up and move, no amount of technology will fix it.

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: Two small children in a park, one reaching up to catch a red balloon.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: Play first, games later: loud, physical, unscripted, and not obviously for anything.
week01-1-play-and-games.credit: Photo by Alaric Sim on Unsplash

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: A retriever standing in a muddy track carrying a branch far longer than itself.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: Nobody taught the dog this. Play rehearses the skills the adult will need.
week01-1-play-and-games.credit: Photo by Jamie Street on Unsplash

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: Runners in lanes on a track, one ahead of the field.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: Agon: competition. The contest is the point, and the rules make it fair enough to be worth winning.
week01-1-play-and-games.credit: Photo by Nicholas Wilson on Unsplash

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: Wooden dice tumbling in mid-air against a black background.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: Alea: chance. The player submits to the roll, which is exactly why it is exciting.
week01-1-play-and-games.credit: Photo by Jonathan Greenaway on Unsplash

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: A stall of ornate Venetian carnival masks in reds, golds and blues.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: Mimicry: make-believe. The mask is permission to be someone else for a while.
week01-1-play-and-games.credit: Photo by Llanydd Lloyd on Unsplash

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: A swing carousel spinning at night, its lights drawn into streaks.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: Ilinx: vertigo. Play that works on the body by disturbing it.
week01-1-play-and-games.credit: Photo by Kiko Camaclang on Unsplash

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: Two people leaning over a brightly coloured board game, mid-turn, cards and money spread around it.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: A game is play with structure: the rules are the rigid part, and the freedom to act inside them is the play.

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: A black chess knight and a white chess knight facing each other on a board.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: A closed formal system, structured conflict, an unequal outcome. Entered willingly.
week01-1-play-and-games.credit: Photo by Hassan Pasha on Unsplash

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: Two players reaching across a dark table strewn with tokens and cards mid-game.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: Inside the magic circle a piece of cardboard is a territory worth fighting over. The lusory attitude is what puts it there.

week01-1-play-and-games.alt: A long dining table laid with candles and flowers in a dark room, before the guests arrive.
week01-1-play-and-games.caption: You can set the table, but you cannot make the party. The game affords the experience; the experience happens between the player and the game.
week01-1-play-and-games.credit: Photo by M F on Unsplash

week02-2-idea-generation.alt: A wall covered in hundreds of clustered sticky notes in green, yellow and pink.
week02-2-idea-generation.caption: Put it on the wall and go for a hundred. Criticism comes later, on a different day.
week02-2-idea-generation.credit: Photo by Hugo Rocha on Unsplash

week02-2-idea-generation.alt: Hand-drawn screen sketches and a connected node diagram spread across a desk.
week02-2-idea-generation.caption: Vary the method: lists, cards, mind maps, cut-ups. Different structures suit different people.
week02-2-idea-generation.credit: Photo by Amélie Mourichon on Unsplash

week02-2-idea-generation.alt: A person pinning hand-drawn sketches onto a wall already covered with them.
week02-2-idea-generation.caption: The writing on the wall: get up, sketch, and let the space remember where the ideas are.
week02-2-idea-generation.credit: Photo by Álvaro Bernal on Unsplash

week02-2-idea-generation.alt: Five gates in a row between a long list of ideas and the list worth testing: can you build it, will people play it, do you love it, can you afford it.
week02-2-idea-generation.credit: Drawn for COMP3540 from Fullerton pp. 181-182

week02-2-idea-generation.alt: A funnel from everything brainstormed, to a shortlist of five to ten, to three ideas, to one game, with a loop back to brainstorm each again.
week02-2-idea-generation.credit: Drawn for COMP3540 from Fullerton pp. 182-188

week02-2-idea-generation.alt: A workshop desk with an annotated design sheet, a pencilled grid and modelling materials.
week02-2-idea-generation.caption: Something changes when you pick one. The flaws get clearer, and so do the reasons you chose it.

week02-2-idea-generation.alt: A paper worksheet mapping out a game with coloured sticks, counters and labels for monsters, treasure and health.
week02-2-idea-generation.caption: Turning an idea into a game starts with the formal elements: rules, procedures, turns, players, goals.

week02-2-idea-generation.alt: A ruled notebook page with a hand-drawn diagram of level sections, annotated with jumps, enemies and checkpoints.
week02-2-idea-generation.caption: Map a typical turn or the core loop as a flowchart. It is the fastest way to find the rule you have not written.

week07-1-agile-game-dev.alt: A person adding a sticky note to a wall plan already dense with notes under handwritten headings.
week07-1-agile-game-dev.caption: The backlog is a list sorted by priority. Things are added, removed and reordered every sprint.
week07-1-agile-game-dev.credit: Photo by Jo Szczepanska on Unsplash

week07-1-agile-game-dev.alt: A loop from a prioritised backlog through sprint planning, two to four weeks of building, demo day and a retrospective, back to the backlog.
week07-1-agile-game-dev.credit: Drawn for COMP3540 from Schell pp. 103-105 and Fullerton pp. 431-440

week07-1-agile-game-dev.alt: A small team standing and sitting together in a sunlit office, one holding a tablet, mid-discussion.
week07-1-agile-game-dev.caption: Scrum: ten minutes, standing up. What I did, what I am doing, what is in my way. Solutions afterwards.
week07-1-agile-game-dev.credit: Photo by Sable Flow on Unsplash

week07-1-agile-game-dev.alt: A burndown chart: work remaining against days in the sprint, with the real line above the ideal one and a jump where scope was added.
week07-1-agile-game-dev.credit: Drawn for COMP3540 from Fullerton pp. 431-440

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: Playtester plays the game unexplained and thinks aloud; you watch without helping and write notes.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.credit: Drawn for COMP3540 from Fullerton ch. 9, pp. 277-310

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: A session timeline: three minutes of introduction, five of warm-up, twenty of play, twenty of discussion and five to wrap up.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.credit: Drawn for COMP3540 from Fullerton ch. 9, pp. 277-310

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: A player at a desktop computer seen from behind over their shoulder, the game on screen.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.caption: Watch from behind, or watch remotely. Either way, ask them to think aloud — and keep reminding them.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.credit: Photo by ELLA DON on Unsplash

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: Two people sitting across a table in conversation, one listening with hands folded.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.caption: The discussion afterwards is half the session. Probe for appeal, challenge and understanding — and do not defend the game.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.credit: Photo by LinkedIn Sales Solutions on Unsplash

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: Two players seen from behind, side by side, watching a split-screen game on a television.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.caption: Group dynamics are good for generating ideas and bad for evaluating them. Test individually when you want the truth.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.credit: Photo by Emily Wade on Unsplash

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: Hands moving a pipe-cleaner character across a paper prototype during a workshop.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.caption: Playtest before you think you are ready. The first one always finds something the tenth would not.

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: A hand writing on a clipboard, lit against a dark background.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.caption: You will remember what you hoped to hear. Write down what actually happened.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.credit: Photo by Vladislav Igumnov on Unsplash

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: A note-taking form in three parts: in-game observations while they play, post-game questions after they play, revision ideas after they leave.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.credit: Drawn for COMP3540 from Fullerton ch. 9, pp. 277-310

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: A dark analytics dashboard of histograms and time-series charts on a laptop screen.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.caption: Numbers tell you what happened, never why. Decide what you want to know before you measure anything.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.credit: Photo by Luke Chesser on Unsplash

week09-2-conducting-playtesting.alt: A workshop desk with a small paper prototype set up mid-game beside pens and spare pieces.
week09-2-conducting-playtesting.caption: A control situation: set the board to the moment you care about and play only that, as many times as you need.
